articles.title: The reasons Norway might reject your Norwegian citizenship application
articles.content:
Add The Local as a preferred source
    
                        
                                        
                        Norwegian citizenship comes with a hefty application fee and plenty of requirements. There are several reasons why the Norwegian Directorate of Immigration might reject an application.

Lifetime enrollment in the Norwegian National Insurance Scheme, the ability to live in Norway for as long as you wish, and returning to Norway after a few years away without going through the immigration process are some of the many benefits of Norwegian citizenship.

Norwegian citizenship doesn’t come easy, though. In addition to waiting years to become eligible, you will have to pass language and citizenship tests, provide a criminal record certificate, verify your identity and meet the requirements for permanent residence if you don’t hold it already.

This is all before you pay 6,500 kroner to apply for Norwegian citizenship.

So, what are the reasons why the Norwegian Directorate of Immigration (UDI) turns down applications?

This applies not just to your citizenship application but also to your entire stay. If you bend the rules when it comes to the residence requirements, you could find your citizenship application rejected.

Even if your application is successful, you will find your citizenship revoked later if the UDI finds out. The UDI will still revoke your citizenship, even if you are the one who decides to come clean to them.

Should the authorities have reason to believe that you have provided incorrect information on any residence or citizenship applications, they will typically invite you for an interview with the police or notify you of your revocation in advance.

READ MORE: How Norway can revoke residency and citizenship over wrong details

This one might seem obvious, but it can happen relatively easily. One of the most common reasons for a foreign national having their citizenship rejected is not passing the citizenship or social studies test (in Norwegian).

For the citizenship test, you must answer 24 out of 36 multiple-choice questions correctly.

The social studies test is taken by those who typically have been through the social studies course for immigrants.

Language-wise, you will generally have to have passed an oral test in Norwegian at  B1 level.

Another common pitfall is the criminal record certificate. Criminal record certificates are only valid for three months. The certification proves that you haven’t been convicted of any crimes and are not disqualified from applying for citizenship.

As the certificate can only be valid for three months, the UDI advises that you shouldn’t order the certificate until you have an appointment to hand in your documents to the police. This reduces the likelihood of the certificate expiring before your documents are handed in.

Failure to meet any of the citizenship requirements will result in your application being turned down. You must also hold a valid residence permit whilst applying for citizenship.

Remember that under standard rules, you must have stayed in Norway for a total of eight of the past eleven years and held residence permits that were each valid for at least one year.

On the UDI website, you can learn how to calculate residence periods in exception cases. However, as there is currently a proposal to amend the Citizenship Act, which could alter how qualifying residence time is measured, these requirements may change in the future.

READ MORE: What will Norway's plan to toughen citizenship rules mean for you?

Being convicted of a criminal offence that results in a fine or prison sentence will bar you from being eligible for citizenship for a set period of time.

The disqualification period can range from 2.5 years up to 39 years, depending on the severity of your punishment. You can see an overview of the disqualification rules on the UDI website.

Those who have received fixed penalty notices rather than criminal fines will not be disqualified. Those who have had charges or cases dropped are also not disqualified.

An example of a fixed penalty notice would be a fine for minor or moderate speeding.

To be eligible for citizenship, you also need to be eligible for permanent residence at the same time, which can make matters confusing.

For many, the easiest way around this is to just hold permanent residence as proof of eligibility while applying for citizenship.

The key thing to look out for when it comes to citizenship is the minimum income requirements for non-EEA permanent residence applicants.

One of the requirements for permanent residence applications for non-EEA nationals is that you will need to have fulfilled the income requirements for the previous 12 months and that you cannot have received financial assistance (økonomisk sosialhjelp) during the prior 12 months.

Israel, som hevder Hamas har rustet opp igjen og gjennomført angrep i strid med våpenhvilen, har trappet opp angrepene mot gruppen de siste ukene.

Hamas avviser anklagene og hevder Israel undergraver våpenhvilen.

articles.content:

Utbetalingen er på 90 dollar per person, tilsvarende rundt 865 norske kroner, melder NTB.

Medicare er USAs offentlige helseordning for eldre og uføre, der del B dekker legebesøk og poliklinisk behandling.

Ifølge Trump skal utbetalingene finansieres av et statlig fond og avtaler som sikrer Medicare like lave medisinpriser som i andre rike land.

articles.title: Did you know that Oslo has its own Mona Lisa?
articles.content:
Add The Local as a preferred source
    
                        
                                        
                        Whether you're an art lover visiting Oslo or a local looking for something different to do, the Norwegian capital holds a rather fun surprise for you.

Yes, you read that correctly: the Mona Lisa and Norway in the same sentence.

The Nasjonalmuseet (Oslo’s National Museum) has its own 17th-century version of the Mona Lisa.

Painted by an unknown artist, this intriguing replica is currently on display in Room 061 as part of the 'Moods and emotions' exhibition.

With autumn here and rainy days ahead, it’s a great time to pop in and catch a glimpse of Leonardo da Vinci's famous masterpiece (or at least a historic copy of it) and see that mysterious smile up close, right in the centre of Oslo.

You are sure to find it much less crowded than in Paris.

The National Museum is Norway’s largest collection of art, architecture and design. If you fancy a visit, you can find the museum’s opening hours here.

articles.content:

                        Norway plans to spend 96 million kroner more on integration, Bergen records its warmest day of the year, all the big October changes, and more news on Thursday.

Norway plans to spend an extra 96 million kroner on Norwegian language classes and integration efforts

The Norwegian government plans to add 96 million kroner to its integration budget in the proposed 2027 national budget.

Speaking during a visit to an organisation in Stavanger, as reported by state broadcaster NRK, Minister of Labour and Inclusion Kjersti Stenseng said the money would support several initiatives, emphasising that learning Norwegian is the most important factor for foreign residents to enter the workforce.

"The most important success factor now for entering the workforce is language. It's about good Norwegian language training. That's why we want to spend more resources on this," Stenseng said.

Most of the extra funding will go to helping immigrant women find jobs and supporting Ukrainian refugees, with 30 million kroner and 32 million kroner set aside for these groups respectively.

Another 17.7 million kroner will be used to make Norwegian language training more flexible and better suited to individual needs, and 2.5 million kroner will fund a new system for assessing oral Norwegian exams .

The remaining funds will support a trial programme for women who came to Norway through family reunification and promote diversity in state enterprises.

"The government is committed, but it also sets requirements in its integration policy. We expect those who come to Norway to learn Norwegian, get a job and become part of the community," explained Stenseng.

The proposed package will be formally presented as part of the 2027 state budget proposal and remains subject to negotiation in parliament.

Norwegian vocabulary: norskopplæring - Norwegian language training

​Norway sees highest number of road deaths in ten years

According to preliminary figures from the Norwegian Public Roads Administration, 95 people have lost their lives in road accidents in the first nine months of this year. That is eleven more than during the same period last year.

In September alone, twelve people died on Norwegian roads.

"What stands out most is that half of those who died on Norwegian roads in September were under 30 years old," said Svein Ringen, acting head of road safety at the Norwegian Public Roads Administration, in a press release.

The counties with the highest numbers of fatalities are Akershus, Innlandet, and Vestland.

Norwegian vocabulary: dødstall - number of fatalities

​Bergen records warmest day of the year on the last day of September

Bergen, a city far better known for its relentless rain, had an unexpected late-season surprise on Wednesday, reaching its highest temperature of the year at 26.1C. This broke the previous summer record of 26C, set on August 26th.

The unusually warm weather was caused by fønvind, a warm, dry wind that heats up quickly as it moves down from the mountains into the lowlands, newspaper Aftenposten reported.

According to the Norwegian Meteorological Institute, unseasonably mild conditions are expected across parts of Western and Northwestern Norway into early October.

"The temperature in particular will be quite high, around 20 degrees. Thursday is October 1st, and it is unusual for such high temperatures to occur then," said state meteorologist Unni Nilssen.

Norway drops plans to cut regional flights and close airports in the north

Transport Minister Kamzy Gunaratnam has confirmed that the government will keep all regional air routes and small airports in Northern Norway open.

“I would like to reiterate that for the Labour Party government it is important that people can live good lives throughout the country. Therefore, we will maintain the current flight routes, and no airports will be closed,” said Minister of Transport Kamzy Gunaratnam in a press release.

This decision comes after strong local opposition to a consultant report that suggested cutting routes, which could have put airports in Vardø, Mosjøen, Namsos, Stokmarknes, and Røst at risk, according to Aftenposten.

​October in Norway: A month of political shifts, shorter (and darker) days and winter prep

October is a time of big changes in Norway, with lots of political activity alongside the practical realities of autumn life.

On the political stage, Stortinget officially opens its 171st parliamentary session with the Constituent Meeting on October 1st, followed by the Ceremonial State Opening on October 2nd.

After that, the government will present its proposed 2027 State Budget (Statsbudsjettet), which will set the economic plan for the coming year.

Also, time is running out to have your say on proposed changes to Norway’s citizenship requirements.

For residents, the shift into mid-autumn brings noticeable changes to daily routines.

The days are getting much shorter, daylight saving time ends as clocks go back, and motorists are turning their attention to winter tyre changes.

articles.content:
Add The Local as a preferred source
    
                        
                                        
                        October is a key month to see how things unfold in Norway for the following year. With the question of integration high on the agenda and many needs still unmet, foreign residents should pay close attention to the upcoming 2027 budget negotiations.

The Norwegian government plans to add 96 million kroner to its integration budget as part of the upcoming 2027 State Budget (Statsbudsjettet).

As is customary every October, the government presents its proposed package to parliament (Stortinget).

Since the Labour-led administration is a minority government, the proposal will need to go through negotiations in parliament to get enough votes for approval before Christmas. However, given integration policy remains a key priority area across the political spectrum, the proposal may find support from other parties.

Under the proposal, the extra funding would cover several important areas. The largest sum would go to helping immigrant women find work through the Jobbsjansen initiative, and to supporting Ukrainian refugees through the Norwegian Directorate of Integration and Diversity (IMDi), with 30 million and 32 million kroner allocated to each, respectively.

Minister of Labour and Inclusion Kjersti Stenseng told Norwegian broadcaster NRK during a visit to Stavanger that learning Norwegian is the most important element for foreign residents who want to join the workforce.

"The most important success factor now for entering the workforce is language. It's about good Norwegian language training. That's why we want to spend more resources on this," Stenseng said.

Based on this, another 17.7 million kroner would be used to make Norwegian language training more flexible and better tailored to individual needs, and 2.5 million kroner would go towards a new system for assessing oral Norwegian exams.

The rest of the funds would support a pilot programme for women who arrived in Norway through family reunification (8.8 million kroner) and promote diversity in state enterprises (5 million kroner).

"The government is committed, but it also sets requirements in its integration policy. We expect those who come to Norway to learn Norwegian, get a job and become part of the community," said Stenseng.

Hildegunn Fandrem, a professor of special education at the Learning Environment Centre at the University of Stavanger (UiS), told NRK that politicians should take a broader approach.

"We place a heavy focus on Norwegian language training itself and language acquisition. I believe there is still room for improvement when it comes to focusing on participation and social inclusion. This means we also need to look at how language training is structured—that is another crucial aspect of successfully integrating people," said the professor.

articles.title: Overqualified and underpaid: The reality facing Norway's foreign workers
articles.content:
Add The Local as a preferred source
    
                        
                                        
                        Four in ten highly educated immigrants in Norway are currently employed in roles below their skill level. This mismatch takes a personal and financial toll on these workers and means Norway misses out on valuable talent.

Relocating to Norway often comes with high expectations, yet for thousands of foreign professionals, arrival marks the beginning of an uphill struggle.

A  very common story in Norway is that even with Master’s degrees and years of experience, many newcomers (or even long time residents) cannot break into their own field.

Given Norway’s high cost of living, immediate income is an absolute necessity. As a result, highly qualified individuals are forced to take up jobs in cleaning, hospitality or retail.

Stories of former lawyers with fifteen years of legal experience cleaning houses or experienced engineers delivering food are far from rare and unfortunately not anecdotal. They reflect an everyday reality for a big portion of Norway’s international workforce.

A study from Statistics Norway (SSB) shows that these personal stories are part of a bigger ongoing structural problem.

Data shows that in 2025, 93,000 immigrants with higher education in Norway worked in jobs that did not match their qualifications. This made up 40 percent of all foreign workers with higher education degrees.

This means many immigrants are employed in roles with lower educational requirements that are completely unrelated to the fields they spent years studying and specialising in.

The highest rate of overqualification is found among non-European immigrants.

Nevertheless, the official total of 93,000 understates the true scale of the issue as SSB does not count foreign workers who have lived in Norway for less than two years. If new arrivals were included, many of whom take any job at first, the total would be much higher.

In short, the 93,000 figure represents merely a baseline rather than the full scale of the issue.

READ ALSO: Foreigners in Norway face '60 percent' lower chance of promotion

While the proportion of overqualified foreign workers has remained stable at around 40 percent over the past decade, the total number of people affected has gone up significantly.

As overall immigration has increased, the total count of overqualified foreign professionals rose from 73,000 in 2021 to 93,000 in 2025.

From 2022 to 2025, the number of overqualified foreign workers grew by 23 percent, which is a bit faster than the 20 percent growth in the total foreign workforce.

This increase happened mostly because many displaced Ukrainians entered the job market quickly and many of them have higher education degrees but started out in entry-level jobs.

While national economic reports frequently highlight rising average wages and strong purchasing power in Norway, many foreign workers feel these numbers do not match their reality.

Overqualified foreign workers had a median monthly wage of 43,840 kroner, while those in jobs that matched their qualifications earned 66,150 kroner.  This means qualified foreign talent loses over 22,000 kroner every month, adding up to more than 267,000 kroner lost per year!

However, the data reveals another systemic disparity that international residents face in Norway.

Overqualified foreign workers also earn less than overqualified workers in the general population. The median monthly salary for all overqualified workers was 49,340 kroner, which is 12.5 percent more than what overqualified foreign workers make.

Foreign professionals who manage to secure relevant positions earn a 51 percent salary premium over their overqualified peers.

In the case of Ukranians in Norway, the reality is even harsher. In 2025, overqualified immigrants with a Ukrainian background had a median monthly salary of  39,210 kroner (around 26,000 kroner less each month).

Most overqualified workers get jobs in sectors that require less education and have more flexible hiring processes.

In 2025, about 31,000 overqualified immigrants worked in retail, hospitality and catering. Areas where jobs with lower wage levels are more frequent.

Approximately 21,000 overqualified immigrants worked in the health and social care industries.

On the bright side, in the Manufacturing, Construction and Energy sector, overqualification rates have steadily dropped since 2018.  Driven by Norway's growing need for technical experts, foreign engineers and specialists now find it easier to get jobs that match their qualifications.

READ MORE: Which industries employ the most workers in Norway?

Besides the financial loss, this situation is emotionally hard for foreign professionals.

Moving to Norway often means taking a big step back in their careers, losing the professional identity they worked so hard to build. Starting over and taking entry-level jobs just to get by causes frustration, anxiety and stress.

Losing professional status so quickly can also hurt self-esteem and often leads to mental health challenges in the first years after moving.

For former lawyers, architects, or teachers, working as cleaners or waiters is a tough psychological blow. It makes adjusting to a new country even harder, and many in this situation quietly wonder: What am I actually doing in Norway?

READ ALSO: What should you do if your boss or landlord in Norway is exploiting you?

On paper, employment rates among immigrants may have improved. However, this reliance on quick job placement also hides deeper economic vulnerabilities.

Many studies show that not deploying talent already in the country can be costly for national productivity and society as a whole.

Holding 93,000 academics, engineers, educators and specialists in low-skilled roles represents a major economic loss in unutilised human capital. This is especially true now, as Norwegian industries urgently need more qualified workers.

articles.title: From boning to fokk: The Norwegian words that will shock English speakers
articles.content:
Add The Local as a preferred source
    
                        
                                        
                        Moving to a new country always comes with a learning curve, but for English speakers in Norway, the local language can lead to some truly surprising and hilarious moments, as Irene Andrade explains.

Due to a mix of shared Germanic roots and, in other cases, some funny coincidences, several entirely innocent Norwegian words and traditional names can sound rude, strange, bizarre or even inappropriate to foreigners.

While learning Norwegian and trying to meet the locals, I’ve had plenty of laughs over these awkward moments (though they make for great anecdotes later).

In the world of driving and transportation, Norwegian vocabulary is an absolute minefield for English speakers.

This coincidence gave birth to one of the most famous memes in Norwegian history.

During an international interview, the legendary Norwegian rally driver Petter Solberg tried to explain a racing accident by translating literally: "It’s not the fart that kills, it’s the smell."

What he actually meant to say in Norwegian was, "It's not the speed that kills, it's the crash" (Det er ikke farten som dreper, det er smellet).

Instead, he delivered a timeless joke that has even inspired comedy sketches on NRK, Norway’s national TV channel.

Una publicación compartida de Unlock Norway (Gabriella Mikiewicz) (@unlocknorway)

If a Norwegian tells you they spent the whole Sunday "boning", do not panic. They were simply polishing or waxing their floors (å bone gulvet).

However, they should be careful with their spelling and context when using the expression in an office setting (especially at a state agency in Norway), as shown in this (possibily fake) photo shared with The Local. We probably do not need to explain why context matters so much here.

This word can trip up English speakers in two ways. In winter, it means drifting or blowing snow. When storms hit Norway, meteorologists often warn about heavy fokk in the mountains (the usual term is snøfokk).

At sea, en fokk is a foresail on a sailboat, with types like stormfokk (storm jib) or rullefokk (roller jib).

This means dirt or rubbish. It’s also a mild swear word, like "crap", and you’ll hear it in the phrase wishing fishermen good luck: Skitt fiske!

The tricky part is the pronunciation. In most Norwegian dialects, when "sk" comes before an "i", it sounds just like the English word "shit".

This word means a dot, but it’s also used for a penalty point on your driving licence.

Telling an English speaker you got a prikk from the police will definitely require some immediate context.

This word translates to boiling or cooking; however, for some English speakers, reading it can instantly cause a double-take.

It also happens to be the name of one of Norway’s most famous floating saunas (KOK), which can lead to some funny misunderstandings. Asking your British or American friend to "spend a warm afternoon inside the hot KOK" might not be the best icebreaker.

In Norwegian, ass is a very common slang abbreviation for the word altså (which can have several meanings, including "though").

Used at the end of a sentence for emphasis, it can also be a way of sounding cool and more modern, meaning "dude" or "man".

For example, "Det var en kul fest, ass" translates to "That was a cool party, man". However, when Norwegians casually carry this over into English conversations, sentences like "She was great, ass" can leave foreigners a bit confused.

Some of Norway’s oldest and most respected names can get lots of laughs abroad. If you already live in Norway and have met a few locals, you have almost certainly had that awkward moment of thinking, "Sorry, could you repeat that?"

It is an ancient male name derived from the Old Norse word for the "point of an arrow or sword." Unfortunately, introducing yourself in London or New York with "Hi, I'm Odd" usually leaves people wondering what’s so strange about you.

Fun fact, 15,904 men have Odd as part of their first name in Norway. I checked.

Then we have the opposite side of the coin with the name Even.

While perfectly normal in Norway, the absolute peak of this phonetic coincidence was shared by a Reddit user who confirmed: "My neighbour's name is literally Odd Even..."

This is the Norwegian variant of the classic name Simon.

It’s a common and respected name across Scandinavia, with 8,652 men named Simen in Norway.

However, because it shares its exact pronunciation with the male biological term in English, international business introductions can lead to some highly uncomfortable situations.

As one Reddit user shared: "I laughed so much when I met my first Simen in Norway. I was like wtf, why doesn't anyone else notice it?!"

Those were the names that first caught my eye, but then I stumbled upon a question online that I just couldn't ignore: “Wondering if there are any Bent Christians out there?”

I couldn't leave it at that. And well, I'm so glad I looked it up. There are exactly 12 men in Norway whose only first name is indeed Bent Christian.

Are we forgetting any? Have you had a "WTF" moment while living or travelling in Norway? Let us know in the comments and (pretty please!) share your photos.

articles.content:
Mannen (51) fra Sunnmøre, som ble dømt til tvungent psykisk helsevern for drapet på Sigrid Giskegjerde Schjetne i 2013, begjærer seg løslatt. Det skriver Dagbladet.

27. oktober skal mannen møte i Sunnmøre tingrett for å få vurdert om dommen på tvungent psykisk helsevern skal forlenges i tre nye år.

Mannens forsvarer, Ida Andenæs Mehren, bekrefter overfor Dagbladet at han nå for første gang vil begjære seg løslatt.

Statsadvokat Ingvild Thorn Nordheim sier til avisen at det er en ordinær forlengelsessak som skal vurderes av domstolen.

Påtalemyndigheten mener at han ikke bør løslates på grunn av gjentakelsesfare.
